title: Beyond global mean temperature: increasing asymmetry of global warming in past and future climate change
abstract: Global surface warming is recognized for its spatial asymmetry, which drives the complexity of climate change impacts. However, solely relying on average surface temperature change ($${\Delta T}_{{mean}}$$) as an indicator of climate change may obscure this asymmetry. Here, going beyond $${\Delta T}_{{mean}}$$, we quantify the long-term change in global warming asymmetry and its implications for climate mitigation. Results reveal a significant increase in warming asymmetry (0.18–0.29 °C3/decade) since 1900. Among 58 IPCC reference regions, the Arctic Ocean, Northwest North America, and Russian Regions contribute only 48% of this trend, with other Northern Hemisphere mid-high latitudes accounting for an additional 35%. Climate models project an emission-dependent nonlinear acceleration of warming asymmetry, with trends under SSP 5-8.5 being approximately 3–8 times greater than those under SSP2-4.5 and SSP1-2.6. Consequently, the global surface temperature change deviates from its original Gaussian distribution toward a highly skewed bimodal distribution. This increasing asymmetry implies a widening “divergence” within the climate system that is dependent on emission levels, including the gap between the $${\Delta T}_{{mean}}$$ and those observed across the majority of regions. Without rigorous emission reductions, this gap could foster cognitive biases in public awareness toward climate change, undermining public acceptance of climate mitigation policies.
problem: Solely relying on average surface temperature change (ΔΤmean) obscures the increasing spatial asymmetry of global warming, which misrepresents the warming experienced by most regions and can foster cognitive biases that undermine public acceptance of climate mitigation policies.
method: This study quantifies the increasing asymmetry of global warming by constructing spatial probability density functions and an asymmetry index based on the third statistical moment, which is used to identify contributions from different regions and project future changes under various emission scenarios.
task: The task is to quantify the long-term change in global warming asymmetry using historical observations and climate model projections, and to analyze its implications for climate mitigation and public perception.

innovation: This paper quantifies the increasing asymmetry of global warming since 1900, showing it will accelerate nonlinearly with future emissions, which skews temperature distributions and undermines the reliability of the global mean temperature metric for assessing climate change and its impacts.

We also analyzed the CMIP6 model-simulated global surface temperature anomalies from the historical scenario (1850–2014) and different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5). For the historical scenario, we retained the results of 29 CMIP6 models (Supplementary Table S1), and the multi-model ensemble mean of 29 CMIP6 models referred to as MME.

We find that most climate models tend to overestimate global warming asymmetry. Although all models successfully capture the historical ATmean and global median surface temperature change (∆Tmedian) (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. S5a-b), over 90% of the models overestimate the trend in asymmetry index. The multi-model ensemble mean (MME) trend of the asymmetry index (0.44°C³/decade) exceeds twice that of the observation (0.19°C³/decade) during 1900–2014 (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Text S3, Fig. S5c).
